title: Number of Different Integers in a String
statement:
The string `word` is made of lowercase English letters and digits. Treat every letter as a separator: what remains is a sequence of maximal blocks of consecutive digits, each block naming a non-negative integer.

Return how many distinct integers these blocks name. Leading zeros do not matter, so `"7"`, `"07"` and `"007"` all name the same integer. A block may be far longer than any built-in number type can hold.
constraints: word contains only digits and lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

The integers can be hundreds of digits long, so converting them to numbers would lose precision or overflow. There is no need to: once leading zeros are dropped, two digit blocks name the same integer exactly when their remaining text is identical. So scan the string once, cut out each digit block without its leading zeros, and count the distinct texts with a set.

## Approach

1. Keep a set `seen` and an index `i` that walks through `word`.
2. If `word[i]` is a letter, step over it.
3. Otherwise a digit block starts here. First skip its leading `'0'` characters.
4. Mark `start` and advance `i` past the remaining digits.
5. Add `word.slice(start, i)` to `seen`. A block made only of zeros becomes the empty string, which stands for `0`.
6. Return `seen.size`.

## Example 1, step by step

`word = "a123bc34d8ef34"`. Skip `a`; the block `123` has no leading zeros, so add `"123"`. Skip `b`, `c`; add `"34"`. Skip `d`; add `"8"`. Skip `e`, `f`; the block `34` adds `"34"` again, which the set already holds. `seen` is `{"123", "34", "8"}`, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each character is visited once, and slicing and hashing the blocks costs O(n) in total.
- Space: O(n) for the stored blocks.

## Pitfalls

- `parseInt` or `Number` round long blocks: `123456789012345678901` and `123456789012345678902` would wrongly look equal.
- Stripping zeros from `"000"` leaves nothing; it must still count as the integer `0` (here, the empty string).
- A block may sit at the very end of `word`; the inner loops must stop at `n`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | distinct blocks with their leading zeros removed |
| `n` | length of `word` |
| `i` | current position in `word` |
| `start` | first significant digit of the current block |

narration.2: A set keeps each distinct integer text once.
narration.7: Is this character a letter rather than a digit?
narration.8: Letters only separate blocks, so skip it.
narration.11: A digit block starts here; skip its leading zeros first.
narration.14: The significant part of the block begins at this position.
narration.15: Move past the rest of the digits in this block.
narration.18: Store the block without leading zeros; an all-zero block becomes the empty string, meaning 0.
narration.20: The number of distinct texts is the number of different integers.
